# Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-10-22 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## How it works

- [statement] MongoDB recommends creating one MongoClient per process and reusing it for all operations in that process. Each MongoClient has a connection pool for each server in the topology, plus up to two monitoring connections per server. Cloud Run scales each revision to the number of instances needed for incoming requests. If each instance runs its own application process (an inference, not stated by either source), then each instance has its own client and pools, and the service's potential connection count grows with the number of active instances and the connected topology. This is a capacity inference; it does not mean every pool reaches its ceiling. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ ; https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-concurrency — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-concurrency, https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances
- [statement] Cloud Run's maximum concurrent requests setting limits the number of requests processed simultaneously by a given instance. It is not a limit on MongoDB sockets. For the same request volume, lower concurrency forces Cloud Run to use more instances, while higher concurrency can lead to fewer active instances if the application handles parallel work. Because MongoDB client pools are per client (per process) and each pool opens sockets per server, concurrency affects the number of pools only indirectly, by changing the number of instances. This last step is an inference. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-concurrency ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ — https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-concurrency · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] In a Node.js Cloud Run service, follow the driver's one-MongoClient-per-process reuse recommendation and place the reusable client outside per-request logic. Google's Cloud Run guide says global-scope objects can be reused by later requests on the same instance, but whether an individual request benefits from that reuse cannot be known ahead of time. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ ; https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/tips/general — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/tips/general
- [statement] Cloud Run concurrency and maximum-instance settings affect the connection envelope: lower concurrency can require more instances for the same traffic, and a maximum-instance setting can limit connections to a backing database but may be exceeded briefly during traffic spikes. Set these controls against the application's tested concurrency and Atlas connection budget, with headroom for temporary scale-out. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-concurrency ; https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances — https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/about-concurrency · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances, https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/databases/best-practices-and-tutorial-using-google-cloud-functions-mongodb-atlas
- [statement] Google documents the Cloud Run maximum-instance setting as a way to limit connections to a backing database and recommends a service-level cap. The configured maximum can be exceeded briefly during traffic spikes, and separate revision limits can overlap during deployments, so a pool budget should include headroom. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances ; https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances-limits — https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/max-instances-limits

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Every MongoClient instance has a built-in connection pool for each server in the MongoDB topology, and each MongoClient also opens up to two monitoring connections per server. Because the pools belong to individual clients, estimate Atlas connection pressure across all simultaneously live clients rather than treating one Cloud Run service as one pool. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/databases/best-practices-and-tutorial-using-google-cloud-functions-mongodb-atlas, https://www.linkedin.com/posts/revelapp_mongodb-serverless-cloudrun-activity-7349493964648951808-1XxD
- [statement] Atlas sets concurrent open-connection limits by cluster tier and class; the limits apply per node, or per mongos router for sharded clusters. Atlas documents new-connection-per-second limits separately, with applicability depending on tier and MongoDB version, and says its autoscaling responds to memory and compute use rather than connection count by itself. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/atlas-limits/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Revel's public field report describes multiple Cloud Run Spring Boot services connecting to Atlas and attributes near-cap connection counts during scale-out to each container holding its own pool. The report's suggested pool, concurrency, and instance settings were proposals for that workload, not general defaults or validated results. (low confidence) — https://www.linkedin.com/posts/revelapp_mongodb-serverless-cloudrun-activity-7349493964648951808-1XxD
- [statement] The current Node.js driver documentation says each MongoClient has a pool for each server, opens application sockets on demand, defaults maxPoolSize to 100 per pool, and opens up to two additional monitoring connections per server. The 100 value is a per-server ceiling, not the number every Cloud Run instance necessarily opens. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-22) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/node/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/
- [statement] A May 2022 Stack Overflow question reports up to 130 Atlas connections while its author saw five or six Cloud Run instances. The author's accepted self-answer proposes rapid scale-out and Mongoose's pool ceiling as the explanation. This is one author's workload report and proposed diagnosis, not a measured general connection count per Cloud Run instance. (low confidence) (verified as of 2022-05-07) Sources: https://api.stackexchange.com/2.3/questions/72086236?site=stackoverflow&filter=withbody ; https://api.stackexchange.com/2.3/questions/72086236/answers?site=stackoverflow&filter=withbody — https://api.stackexchange.com/2.3/questions/72086236?site=stackoverflow&filter=withbody · keywords: Cloud Run Atlas Connection Pooling · also: https://api.stackexchange.com/2.3/answers/72154147?site=stackoverflow&filter=withbody
